name: Crimson Escarpment
geological_features: A single massive escarpment dividing the planet into high and low hemispheres
Iron-oxide-rich soils giving the terrain its crimson coloration
Seasonal flooding plains on the lower hemisphere
description: Crimson Escarpment takes its name from the colossal geological cliff that wraps around the planet's equator, rising nearly eight kilometers from the southern lowlands to the northern highlands. The iron-rich soil paints everything in shades of rust and vermillion. Small seas collect in the lower hemisphere, fed by meltwater cascading down the great escarpment.

The atmosphere is clean and sharp, with lower oxygen content at the highland elevations. Wind funnels along the escarpment face, creating permanent updrafts that carry red dust high into the stratosphere. Sunsets last for hours as light filters through the suspended particulate, painting the sky in deep scarlet.

Microbial mats carpet the seasonal flood plains, forming thick russet crusts that crack and reform with each wet-dry cycle. These organisms are iron metabolizers, and their activity over billions of years is responsible for the planet's distinctive coloration. No complex life has emerged, though the microbial ecosystem is remarkably diverse and robust.

Crimson Escarpment's iron deposits are vast but low-grade, making it a marginal mining prospect. Its real value lies in the study of its microbial biosphere, which may offer insights into early-stage planetary biology. The escarpment itself presents engineering challenges for any settlement, but the dramatic terrain has not deterred a handful of frontier outposts from taking root on the highland rim.
